note: Our own words for the functions of the firmware that the sources bind, for docs/firmware-interfaces.md (tools/interfaces.py makes the page). For an address: a short name, its group, what the caller hands over and gets back, and the threads our code calls it on. Only what a caller needs is said here; how a function works inside is not (CONTRIBUTING.md, "Writing about the firmware"). Every address belongs to OS 1.7.3.
about: This page lists the functions of the firmware that open-field's own code calls, for OS 1.7.3. For each it says where the function stands, what the caller hands over, what comes back and which thread our code calls it on. It says nothing of how a function works inside: that is not needed to call it, and it is not written down in this repository ([CONTRIBUTING.md](../CONTRIBUTING.md), "Writing about the firmware").
**Every address belongs to one firmware file**, OS 1.7.3. On another version each one has to be found again ([methods](methods.md), "Moving the work to another firmware version").
**How a source binds a function.** Two lines: the function's type, and a name for its address. The type is ours; nothing of the firmware is copied.

**How arguments travel.** The first three go in the registers R0, R1 and R2, the rest on the stack. A result comes back in R0. A function that gives back a structure gets the address for it in P0. The compiler does all of that when the type is right, so a wrong type is a crash: before you bind a function that is not on this page, read how the firmware itself calls it ([methods](methods.md), "Reading a caller before you bind a function").

**The threads.** *The main thread* runs the start-up. *The display thread* draws a frame some sixty times a second; the shared part calls our frame functions from it. *The key thread* hands key presses and knob turns to the mode that is shown. *The audio thread* makes the sound, a block of 64 samples at a time, and must never wait: no log line, no file, no memory asked for there. Where the last column says "ours", it names the threads our code calls the function on today; that it is safe on another thread has not been shown.

log.title: The log
log.about: The unit writes a log into the folder `logs` of its disk. [Methods](methods.md) says how to copy a log off the unit and how to read one.

files.title: Files on the unit's disk
files.about: A path is a C text, counted from the top of the unit's disk, with no slash in front: `user/pk/kit.pack`. There are two families of calls. Use one family for a file from its open to its close.

json.title: JSON values and JSON files
json.about: The firmware keeps its settings as JSON, and so does our code. A JSON value is a small object of 12 bytes in memory the caller provides (our code keeps 16). It owns what it holds: make it with `json_ctor`, give it back with `json_dtor`. What `json_at`, `json_get` and `json_lookup` give back is a reference into another value, not a value of the caller's to destroy. A value has a kind: 0 nothing (null), 1 an integer, 2 an unsigned number, 3 a number with a fraction, 4 a text, 5 true or false, 6 an array, 7 an object. A number read from a file has the kind 2 or 3, never 1: do not test for 1, ask `json_int`.

memory.title: Texts and memory
memory.about: Our code has no library of its own: no `malloc`, no `memcpy`, no division by a variable. What it needs of memory it keeps in its own data, or asks of the firmware with the calls below.

screens.title: Screens, pictures and texts
screens.about: A screen of the firmware is an object with a picture: an SVG text, parsed into a document whose parts can be found by their id, shown, hidden, moved and given a text. Our own screens are made the same way.

keys.title: Keys and the screen that is shown

sounds.title: Sounds and their LFOs
sounds.about: The unit has eight synth sounds and eight drum sounds, in slots 0 to 7 each. Each slot has a record, an object of the firmware's at a fixed address, which holds the sound's document: what the unit saves with the sound. A sound's LFO has a kind (a row of the list under shift and T4), eight words of settings and a switch. Our code changes them through the calls below, the way the unit's own keys do, so that what the unit shows, plays and saves agrees.

0x8c053a20.name: log
0x8c053a20.what: Writes one line into the unit's log. `level`: 3 for a line of information, 2 for a warning, 1 for an error. `file`: a text in the form of a source path; the log shows what stands between its last slash and its dot as the line's tag, so `op1f/mypack.cpp` gives the tag `mypack`. A text without a slash and a dot gives a line with no tag. `line`: a number shown in brackets behind the tag. `format` and the values behind it: as `printf` takes them. A line is cut at about 260 characters, the time and the tag counted.
0x8c053a20.thread: Any thread but the audio thread: keep a count there and print it from a frame function. Ours: the main thread at the start, the display thread, the key thread, the tape's background thread.

0x8c051f9c.name: file_size
0x8c051f9c.what: The size of the file at a path, in bytes; -1 when there is no such file. It writes nothing into the log, so it is the way to ask whether a file is there.
0x8c051f9c.thread: Not the audio thread. Ours: the main thread at the start, the display thread, the disk mode's thread.

0x8fc8a9d8.name: file_open
0x8fc8a9d8.what: Opens a file. `mode` is a text as C's `fopen` takes it; our code hands over the firmware's own text for reading, `rb`, which stands at `0x848daa84`. Gives back a descriptor, a small number that may be 0. A negative number means the open failed, and the function has then written a line into the log itself.
0x8fc8a9d8.thread: Not the audio thread. Ours: the main thread at the start and when a screen is made, and the display thread.

0x8fc8a9a8.name: file_read
0x8fc8a9a8.what: Reads `count` items of `size` bytes into the buffer. Gives back the number of items read. The descriptor is the fourth argument, so it travels on the stack.

0x8c0a3630.name: file_seek
0x8c0a3630.what: Goes to a place in a file opened with `file_open`. The offset is 64 bits wide and is handed over as two words, the low one first. `from`: 0 counts from the file's start, 1 from the present place, 2 from the file's end. Gives back the low word of the new place.

0x8c05206c.name: make_folders
0x8c05206c.what: Makes the folders of a path that are missing. Only a part that a slash ends is made: `user/fx/` makes both folders, `user/fx` makes `user` alone.

0x8fcbefb4.name: file_remove
0x8fcbefb4.what: Removes the file at a path. Gives back 0 when the file is gone.

0x8c051e28.name: dir_open
0x8c051e28.what: Opens a folder to list it. The path has no slash at its end. Gives back a handle, or 0 when the folder cannot be opened.
0x8c051e28.thread: Not the audio thread. Ours: the main thread at the start, the disk mode's thread.

0x8c0a4bd0.name: dir_next
0x8c0a4bd0.what: The next entry of a folder opened with `dir_open`, or 0 at the end. The entry's name is the text that starts 11 bytes into what comes back. Do not count on the order of the entries: our code sorts the names itself.

0x8c085ba8.name: json_ctor
0x8c085ba8.what: Makes a value of a kind in the caller's 12 bytes. Kind 0 makes a null, which becomes an array at its first `json_push`.
0x8c085ba8.thread: Not the audio thread. Ours: the main thread at the start, the display thread, the key thread.

0x8c0844e0.name: json_dtor
0x8c0844e0.what: Gives back what a value holds. Call it for every value made with `json_ctor`, and for none that is a reference.

0x8c0534d0.name: json_read_file
0x8c0534d0.what: Reads a JSON file and parses it into a value the caller has made. Not 0 when the file was read and parsed.

0x8c053168.name: json_write_file
0x8c053168.what: Writes a value as a JSON file. The path is a text object of the firmware (`string_ctor` below), not a C text. The file is written under a spare name in the folder `tmp` and then renamed over the target. 0 comes back when that failed: look at the answer, and make the target's folder first.

0x8c084840.name: json_int
0x8c084840.what: A number as an `int`. It takes all three kinds of number. For any other kind it gives back 0 and writes a line into the log.

0x8c084c22.name: json_size
0x8c084c22.what: How many elements an array has. Ask it of an array only.

0x8c084ee0.name: json_at
0x8c084ee0.what: An array's element by its number, from 0: a reference into the array.

0x8c085068.name: json_has
0x8c085068.what: Not 0 when an object has a member of that name.

0x8c084f74.name: json_get
0x8c084f74.what: An object's member by its name: a reference into the object. Our code asks `json_has` first and never asks for a member that is not there.

0x8c085e84.name: json_lookup
0x8c085e84.what: An object's member by its name, as `json_get` gives it; a member that is not there is made, as a null. The way to add a member: look it up, then assign to it.

0x8c0845b8.name: json_assign
0x8c0845b8.what: Gives a value the content of another. The target may be a reference, such as a member got with `json_lookup`.

0x8c085d54.name: json_push
0x8c085d54.what: Puts a copy of a value at an array's end. A null becomes an array at its first push.

0x8c083b1c.name: json_from_int
0x8c083b1c.what: Makes a value an integer (the kind 1).

0x8c083aec.name: json_from_bool
0x8c083aec.what: Makes a value true or false (the kind 5).

0x8c084430.name: json_from_cstr
0x8c084430.what: Makes a value a text (the kind 4), copied from a C text.

0x8c03e434.name: string_ctor
0x8c03e434.what: Makes a text object of the firmware from a C text, in memory the caller provides (our code keeps 48 zeroed bytes for it). A text of up to fifteen characters lives inside the object, and nothing has to be freed afterwards. Our code keeps its paths that short for this reason: `user/op1f.json` fits, `user/lfo/01.json` does not.
0x8c03e434.thread: Not the audio thread. Ours: the main thread at the start, the display thread, the key thread, the disk mode's thread.

0x8fcc7560.name: alloc
0x8fcc7560.what: A block of the firmware's own heap, the one its screens and pictures come from. It never gives back 0: when the heap has no room, the firmware writes an error into the log and stops. So bound what you ask for (our picture maker asks for a megabyte at most) and give every block back with `free` at `0x8fcc4e10`.
0x8fcc7560.thread: Not the audio thread. Ours: the main thread when a screen is made, and the display thread.

0x8fcc6c30.name: free
0x8fcc6c30.what: Gives back a block got with `alloc` at `0x8fcc5744`.

0x8fcc51fc.name: heap_free
0x8fcc51fc.what: How many bytes of such a heap are not in use, by the heap's number.

0x8c040298.name: parse_svg
0x8c040298.what: Parses a picture, an SVG text that a zero byte ends, into a document. Gives back the document, or 0. Hand it only what the firmware's own pictures use: the path commands M, L, H, V, C, S and z in capitals or small letters, and no attribute its own files lack. A path command it does not know makes it hang, and the unit with it.
0x8c040298.thread: Ours: the main thread when a screen is made, and the display thread.

0x8fc26398.name: screen_ctor
0x8fc26398.what: Makes a screen object in memory the caller provides (our code keeps 64 bytes) and registers it under a number. Register a screen once: a number that is taken stops the firmware. In OS 1.7.3 our code uses the numbers 37, 38 and 77, which are free there. Keep a number below 82: the firmware draws the screens in the order of their numbers, and a screen above 82 is drawn over the shutdown countdown. The object's second word is its document: put the parsed picture there. `name` may be 0.

0x8fc25cc0.name: find_node
0x8fc25cc0.what: Finds a part of a screen's picture by its id. With `optional` not 0 it gives back 0 for a part that is not there, and our code always asks that way. The screen must have its document: look at the object's second word before you ask.

0x8c03dbbe.name: apply_matrix
0x8c03dbbe.what: Gives a part of a picture a transform: nine words, each a number with ten bits behind the point, `[a, b, 0, c, d, 0, e, f, 1024]`, for x' = a·x + c·y + e and y' = b·x + d·y + f. Keep the third, sixth and ninth word at 0, 0 and 1024.

0x8fc25abc.name: label_from_node
0x8fc25abc.what: Turns a part of a picture into a label, an object whose text can be set while the unit runs. The part is a placeholder: it gives the label its place and its colour. The label takes the part's place in the document and comes back; keep it, since the id finds it no more. Our code passes 0 for `kind`: the text then starts at the placeholder's left edge.
0x8fc25abc.thread: Ours: the display thread, once for each label.

0x8fc3aa3c.name: label_text
0x8fc3aa3c.what: Sets a label's text from a C text. A text wider than `max_width` pixels is shortened and gets a mark at its end. An empty text hides the label. Send small letters and digits: the firmware's font has the letters at the small letters' codes and its own signs at the capitals'. Each call asks the heap for memory, so set a text only when it changes; setting the text a label already has changes nothing.

0x8fc3820c.name: label_bounds
0x8fc3820c.what: The box of a label's text as it was last laid out: left, right, top and bottom, each a number with ten bits behind the point. It is the box of the shapes without their stroke, so an upright stroke is 0 wide. The box comes back as a structure, by value: bind the function as one that returns the structure, and the compiler hands over the address for it in P0.

0x8c0b2554.name: request_screen
0x8c0b2554.what: Asks the firmware to show the screen the present mode wants now. The firmware does this itself after every key; our code calls it after a change that no key press follows, such as a timer running out. It takes no argument. From the display thread, call it with interrupts masked for the length of the call: the firmware stops when two threads are inside it at once.
0x8c0b2554.thread: Ours: the key thread, and the display thread with interrupts masked.

0x8fc24ca4.name: shift
0x8fc24ca4.what: Not 0 while the shift key is held.
0x8fc24ca4.thread: Ours: the key thread, the display thread.

0x8fc64c68.name: settings_screen_make
0x8fc64c68.what: Makes a screen of the kind the settings rows KEYBOARD, SYSTEM and MIDI show on the right: up to seven lines, a name and a value each, and one set of seven lines that all such screens share. `screen` is a block of 44 bytes from the allocator; `name` is a text in small letters, which the list on the left shows in capitals. The function writes the screen's table into its first word: our code writes a table of its own over it, its name function first and its draw second. Each call empties the seven shared lines, so make a screen once, at the start.
0x8fc64c68.thread: Ours: the main thread at the start.

0x8fc64de0.name: settings_screen_draw
0x8fc64de0.what: Draws the right side of such a screen: the first lines of the shared seven, as many as the word at `screen + 0xc` says, in the unit's own letters and colours, with the line the word at `screen + 8` names drawn as the chosen one. `context` is what the firmware hands a screen's draw: pass it on as it came.
0x8fc64de0.thread: Ours: the display thread, from our own screen's draw.

0x8fc64c2c.name: settings_line_name
0x8fc64c2c.what: Sets the name on line `line` (0 to 6) of the seven shared lines: a text in small letters, at most 31 characters, shown in capitals. `screen` is not read: the lines are the same for every such screen, so write them right before the draw of the screen they are meant for.
0x8fc64c2c.thread: Ours: the display thread and the key thread.

0x8fc64c08.name: settings_line_value
0x8fc64c08.what: Sets the value on line `line` (0 to 6) of the seven shared lines, as `settings_line_name` sets the name.
0x8fc64c08.thread: Ours: the display thread and the key thread.

0x8c0b68b0.name: knob_item_top
0x8c0b68b0.what: Sets the highest value of one of the unit's knob items, the 32-byte objects the settings' items and line pickers are made of, to `top` whole steps, and holds the item's value to it. KEYBOARD, SYSTEM and MIDI keep their line picker in the row at `row + 4`, with the number of lines less one as its top. The firmware stops when the top is below the item's lowest value.

0x8c0d44b0.name: keyboard_chosen
0x8c0d44b0.what: The settings screen lists its rows on the left; a row is an object whose first word is the address of its table of functions, which the firmware calls on the key thread. This is KEYBOARD's function for its row being chosen (`row`: the row). It writes the row's own three lines into the shared seven, sets the number of lines in the row (the word at `row + 0x2c`) and in its screen, and sets the top of the row's line picker. The firmware calls it through the row's table; our code calls it first from its own function in that word of the table.

0x8c0d4d0c.name: system_chosen
0x8c0d4d0c.what: The same for SYSTEM, with its six lines.

0x8c0d484c.name: midi_chosen
0x8c0d484c.what: The same for MIDI, with its five lines.

0x8c0d45ce.name: keyboard_red
0x8c0d45ce.what: The settings row KEYBOARD's function for a turn of the red knob on line `line` of its row (`row`). `amount` is the turn as the firmware hands it, a float: pass it on as it came. Hand it only the row's own lines, 0 to 2.

0x8c0d5018.name: system_red
0x8c0d5018.what: The same for SYSTEM: only its own lines, 0 to 5.

0x8c0d49d0.name: midi_red
0x8c0d49d0.what: The same for MIDI: only its own lines, 0 to 4.

0x8d4f3c84.name: lfo_words_doc
0x8d4f3c84.what: Writes eight words of LFO settings into the document of the sound whose record is `record`. Follow it with the record's LFO apply (`lfo_apply_synth` or `lfo_apply_drum`), so that the sound plays them.

0x8d4f3d0c.name: lfo_active_doc
0x8d4f3d0c.what: Writes the LFO's switch, `on` 1 or 0, into the document of the sound whose record is `record`. Our code calls it right after `lfo_on_synth` or `lfo_on_drum`, so that the switch the sound plays with is the one it is saved with.

0x8d4f64c0.name: lfo_apply_synth
0x8d4f64c0.what: Makes the synth sound whose record is `record` play the LFO its document holds now, as after a change on the unit's own LFO page.

0x8d4f4f90.name: lfo_apply_drum
0x8d4f4f90.what: The same for a drum sound's record.

0x8d504308.name: lfo_on_synth
0x8d504308.what: Switches the LFO of synth slot `slot` (0 to 7) on (`on` 1) or off (0), as the unit's own key does. It changes the switch the sound plays with; `lfo_active_doc` writes it into the document.
0x8d504308.thread: Ours: the key thread, the display thread.

0x8d5042d8.name: lfo_on_drum
0x8d5042d8.what: The same for drum slot `slot` (0 to 7).

0x8d504290.name: lfo_on_synth_read
0x8d504290.what: Whether the LFO of synth slot `slot` (0 to 7) is on: not 0 when it is.
0x8d504290.thread: Ours: the key thread, the display thread.

0x8d504260.name: lfo_on_drum_read
0x8d504260.what: The same for drum slot `slot` (0 to 7).
0x8d504260.thread: Ours: the key thread, the display thread.

0x8fc275e4.name: lfo_screen_of
0x8fc275e4.what: The number of the screen the unit shows for an LFO of kind `kind`, in the firmware's own numbering of its six kinds, 0 to 5. Our code asks it once for each kind, at its first frame, and knows the LFO pages by those numbers from then on.

0x8d4f221c.name: lookup
0x8d4f221c.what: Finds a row of the unit's catalog of sounds and effects. `database`: which part of the catalog, as the firmware hands it; `key`: the group's key; `name`: the row's name, as the firmware hands it; the row is put into the JSON value `out`. Gives back 0 when there is no such row. Our code calls it from its own function in its place where the master effect's list opens, and then, while the master rides an effect of a pack, puts that effect's id into the row.
